meta.title: Turkish B1
meta.subtitle: 999 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Turkish → English (see the Turkish, recall the meaning) and English → Turkish (see an English meaning, recall the Turkish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 999 words for level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: the Yunus Emre Institute's Turkish Proficiency Exam (TYS) certifies only B2 and C1 and publishes no vocabulary list. The scope of this deck is taken instead from the Turkish as a Foreign Language Teaching Programme (Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı; Türkiye Maarif Foundation, 2nd edition, 2020, approved by Turkey's Ministry of National Education), a CEFR-based syllabus whose B1 tables for secondary school (pp. 265–274, with B1+ on pp. 275–284) are organised in twenty themes: a new course and new friends, school life and the news, entertainment and festivals, food and cooking, the environment, sport, technology, tales and legends, personality, and the online world; and, for B1+, which this deck includes, friends and plans, living together, the news, theatre and cinema, inventions, clothes, famous places, humour, holidays and celebrations, and nature. FROM A2 UP THE PROGRAMME LISTS NO VOCABULARY AT ALL: its A2 table says the vocabulary section was left out so as not to limit the level, and the B1 tables carry none either. What each theme gives instead is its suggested topics — enrolment, elections and clubs, traditional entertainment and music, recipes and table manners, pollution and recycling, competitions and fair play, manuals and complaints, legends and jokes, character and empathy, social media and online shopping, letters, neighbours and solidarity, the economy and health in the news, the stage and advertising, inventors, sizes and returns, historic buildings, cartoons and riddles, festivals and ceremonies, landforms and wildlife. So 304 of the 999 words were written for Folio for those topics, a theme at a time, and are Folio's choice rather than the programme's; 13 more are words its B1 grammar list itself names (dek, rağmen, dolayı, sayesinde, örnek …). This is not an official word list and is not presented as one. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 682 are the commonest words of everyday Turkish, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 9 two-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Turkish builds words by adding suffixes, and a suffix's vowel follows the vowels of the word (vowel harmony) while some stems change before it, so the card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 544 nouns show their plural and five cases — iyilik: iyilikler, iyiliği, iyiliğe, iyilikte, iyilikten, iyiliğin. 145 verbs show the third person of the present, the aorist (the general present), the past and the future — uğramak: uğruyor, uğrar, uğradı, uğrayacak — the aorist's vowel being the one a learner cannot predict. 2 pronouns show their cases. Adjectives do not inflect and carry no forms. Real example sentences come with 995 of the 999 words, three apiece for 982, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Scope: Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı, Türkiye Maarif Vakfı, 2020 (ISBN 978-605-80438-2-4). Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
